title: Der »Sicherheitsschild der Amerikas«
summary: Zwischen Sicherheitsbündnis und politischer Allianz

ai.sum: An SWP analysis examines the security alliance and political partnership in the Americas.

brief.summary: The authors examine the US-led "Shield of the Americas" initiative, launched in March 2026, which combines counter-narcotics, military cooperation and efforts to counter Chinese influence in Latin America and the Caribbean. They argue that the initiative privileges ideologically aligned, right-leaning governments and excludes key regional states such as Brazil, Mexico and Canada, shifting the region from liberal multilateralism toward a hemispheric order under US leadership. The September 2026 declaration added economic goals, including supply chains and critical minerals, and a three-pillar structure. The authors stress that the arrangement lacks a binding action plan and clear implementation steps, so its durability is uncertain and tied to the Trump administration's term. They also note that the framing of cartels as "narco-terrorists" can justify military force, and that Chile's accession sparked a domestic legal dispute over whether the initiative amounts to an international treaty. Many regional governments, they add, are hedging to protect their trade with China and their room for manoeuvre.
brief.argument: The Shield of the Americas is a US-led, ideologically selective hemispheric security order whose binding force and durability remain doubtful, while it offers Europe a chance to win regional partners as diversification partners.
recommendations: Europe should position itself as a reliable diversification partner for Latin American states wary of dependence on Washington.
Partner governments should clarify the legal status of the initiative, as Chile's domestic debate shows the risk of undefined commitments.

title: The Endless Chip War
summary: This exclusive Cogs of War interview is with Rakesh Kumar, the author of Chip Age: How Semiconductors Became the World’s Most Powerful Resource. Rakesh has worked as a co-founder, professor, researcher, and advisor in the chip industry for more than two decades. Chipmaking is an evergreen technology with ever-increasing geopolitical implications, and so we asked him to share his thoughts on his book and the field’s future. Sign Up for Our Newsletter You’ve worked with and…

ai.sum: An interview with Rakesh Kumar discusses semiconductors' geopolitical role and his book Chip Age.

brief.summary: The authors, through an interview with chip researcher Rakesh Kumar, argue that chip wars, shortages and export controls are long-standing features of the industry rather than new phenomena, driven by cyclical demand, fragile efficient supply chains and chips' strategic value. They contend that legacy chip capacity is likely to be exited by leading foundries within a few years, that chip innovation is slowing, and that AI is repeating earlier patterns: value accruing to 'pick and shovel' suppliers, software moats, consolidation, and geopolitical weaponisation. They judge that the Pentagon has little leverage over a globally distributed supply chain, that trust mechanisms fail in wartime, and that chokepoints differ in tractability, with critical minerals and lithography hard to replicate and Intel's revival needing anchor customers.
brief.argument: Chip competition is a recurring structural feature of the industry, and today's AI-driven race will not escape the same constraints of cost, consolidation and dependence on chokepoints that have shaped it since the Cold War.
recommendations: Create three to four time-bound industry-government consortia on innovation targets, open to allies, and make participation a condition for federal chip funding
Pair onshoring and authorised-only sourcing with multi-layered physical and electrical verification and built-in authentication features in critical defence chips
Address critical minerals mainly through friendshoring and allied processing capacity, and pursue next-generation lithography alternatives rather than replicating ASML
Use anchor purchases and direct funding to help Intel reach self-sustaining advanced manufacturing

title: Deception in Mass Autonomous Warfare
summary: “[T]he exigencies of desperate survival do stimulate wise leaders to seek such unorthodox solutions.” —Barton Whaley, StratagemOn the night of Jan. 5, 2025, my first mission in the Pokrovsk command post was to make a fake radio call. We knew Russian forces were listening in. We did not know whether the position our men were due to occupy the next day, the Homar trench at Kotlyne, was still in our hands or if the enemy had already taken it. I did as instructed: I pretended…

ai.sum: A War on the Rocks essay analyses deception tactics in mass autonomous warfare, drawing on Pokrovsk experience.

brief.summary: The author, a French veteran who fought near Pokrovsk, argues that on a battlefield made transparent by drones and sensors, deception must replace concealment as the main way to protect manoeuvre. He draws on his own fake radio call at Kotlyne and on Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi to show that cheap decoys can waste enemy interceptors and shape the enemy's picture. He proposes nesting deception across echelons, managing signatures as a coherent system, and targeting the automated sensing and classification chain as well as the human commander. He also sets out legal limits on decoys, the need for coalition deconfliction, and the trade-off of carrying decoy kit instead of other supplies.
brief.argument: On a sensor-saturated battlefield, deception must be institutionalised across all echelons and aimed at automated classification chains, not just human commanders, and must be governed by cost-effectiveness and legal limits.
recommendations: Nest signature management across echelons, with central control of the signature library and decentralised employment.
Set legal safeguards for decoys, including bans on imitating protected signals, civilian-presence assessments, and time-limited deployments.
Deconflict decoy use within shared situational awareness systems and log and share every deployed signature with partners.
Create battalion-level electromagnetic spectrum operations cells to manage signature fleets and reprogram emitters.
brief.turkey: For Türkiye's own force development, the piece suggests that low-cost decoy and signature management could be a doctrinal and procurement consideration alongside its drone and air-defence programmes.

title: The West Is Thinking Too Small About Ukraine’s Victory
summary: Since fall 2023, Ukraine’s supporters have fallen into a pattern: Ukrainians warn that Russia is targeting its energy infrastructure to prevent them from heating their homes, schools, and businesses in the coming winter. Allies provide insufficient support to Ukraine’s efforts to harden its energy grid and other critical infrastructure. Ukrainians devise new ways to stay warm, stretch the aid they do get as far as it can go, and survive the winter without catastrophic…

ai.sum: A War on the Rocks analysis argues Western support for Ukraine's energy resilience is insufficient ahead of Russia's winter strikes on infrastructure.

brief.summary: The author argues that Western policy on Ukraine is trapped between two short-term modes: crisis responses ('something must be done') and 'one weird trick' fixes such as weapons, territorial concessions, or talks. She contends that Russia's campaign, especially repeated winter strikes on energy, schools, books and connectivity, is a slow attack on Ukrainian society that demands a generational view of victory. Drawing on the co-production model with Denmark and Ukraine's defence tech sector, and on examples like Mariupol State University in exile, she urges sustained, detailed partnerships across education, health and social resilience. Her method is largely experiential and anecdotal, drawing on conversations and the observations of Ukrainian educators, and she calls for policymakers to listen to ordinary Ukrainians and plan for next winter now.
brief.argument: Ukraine's victory is a generational project that Western allies must support through sustained, sector-specific partnerships rather than episodic crisis responses or quick fixes.
recommendations: Replicate the co-production model used with Denmark and defence tech firms across other sectors essential to Ukraine's survival.
Invest now in Ukrainian innovations, such as winter energy and resilience solutions, so they can be deployed at scale before next winter.
Enter long-term partnerships with Ukrainian educational institutions, including those serving students from occupied territories.
Ask Ukrainians at local, civil society and parliamentary levels about their needs and aspirations instead of relying only on ministry officials.

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis argues Trump will define his legacy by how the Russia-Ukraine war ends.

brief.summary: The author argues that Trump's handling of Russia's war in Ukraine will define his foreign policy legacy. He contends that a secure, sovereign Ukraine integrated into Western institutions would be an American strategic win, while abandoning it would carry a generational cost. The piece points to a pattern of concessions to Moscow, including a diesel deal, waived sanctions and tariffs, and a proposed Shenzhen summit excluding Ukraine and Europe, and reads these as risking a 'Yalta 2' style carve-up with Russia and China. The author sees Trump's transactional approach as misreading Putin, whose aim is imperial subordination of Ukraine. He concludes that Trump still has leverage to tie sanctions relief to Russian concessions, sustain Ukraine's defences, and secure European guarantees, and that a durable peace is still possible.
brief.argument: Trump's Russia policy will determine his legacy, and continued concessions to Putin risk a spheres-of-influence settlement that undermines Ukraine, Europe and US leadership.

summary: An emboldened Iran could trigger an IS comeback newspress_en Thu, 10/22/2026 - 13:34 Politics The Islamic State (IS) has been defeated in its original core territories, Syria and Iraq. Despite the US military withdrawal from those states, the United States, its international Anti-IS Coalition, Iraq and Syria have powerful capabilities to keep the terrorist group suppressed. But many of the conditions that led to IS’s explosive growth 12 years ago remain latent: some support…

ai.sum: An analysis argues that an emboldened Iran could enable a resurgence of the Islamic State after the US withdrawal from Iraq and Syria.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Islamic State has been largely defeated in Iraq and Syria, with attacks down to under 50 this year. Its underlying conditions, including Sunni Arab rejection of Iranian and proxy control and some support for violent fundamentalism, remain latent. They contend the most likely trigger for an IS revival would be renewed Iranian expansion into a security vacuum left by a US withdrawal. They say neither Arab states, Europe, Türkiye nor Israel could readily replace Washington in containing Iran, since the US supplies leadership and convening power as well as military strength. Failure by the US and partners in the current campaign against Iran could therefore unleash both Iran and a fresh IS threat.
brief.argument: A failed campaign against Iran and a US withdrawal could let Iranian expansion revive the conditions that allowed IS to emerge.
recommendations: Keep the US and anti-IS coalition's counter-IS capabilities in Iraq and Syria, including OIR's authority to strike high-value targets in Syria.
Continue sustained military assistance, training and equipment for Baghdad.
Recognise that containing Iran requires US leadership and convening power that regional states cannot easily substitute.
brief.turkey: The authors judge Türkiye has little interest in containing Iran beyond its immediate near abroad, which bears on how Ankara would position itself in a post-US-withdrawal Iraq and Syria.

title: Iraq is not in danger of Balkanisation
summary: Iraq is not in danger of Balkanisation newspress_en Thu, 10/22/2026 - 13:29 Politics On 23 September 2026, after a meeting with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al‑Zaidi on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio linked the proliferation of weapons beyond state control to dangers that threaten a country’s unity and political cohesion. This claim is well supported by examples in world history. The most notorious example is…

ai.sum: Al Majalla argues that Iraq is not in danger of Balkanisation despite Marco Rubio's warnings.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the risk of Iraq being Balkanised is a long shot, and they test this against the theory of state collapse. They note that Washington has extended its disarmament deadline for weapons outside state control to June 2027. Prime Minister al-Zaidi has persuaded three armed factions to hand over weapons in exchange for ministerial posts, while Kataib Hezbollah refuses. The authors argue that this 'carrot' approach is narrowing the problem and reducing the likelihood of fragmentation, and that it serves Washington's aim of loosening Shiite factions' ties to Iran. Drawing on Clément's framework, they hold that collapse becomes likely only when domestic fragility converges with withdrawal of external support, and they cite the 2017 Kurdish referendum as a case where foreign opposition, not Baghdad, blocked secession. They conclude that Iraq's deeper problem is a political class that has hollowed out the state since 2003.
brief.argument: Iraq's risk of Balkanisation is receding because the state is co-opting armed factions through political office, though deep domestic fragility remains that would become dangerous if external backing were withdrawn.
recommendations: Use ministerial posts and political participation to bring armed factions into state authority and loosen their ties to Iran.
Keep the disarmament process on track, with the deadline extended to 30 June 2027.
Rebuild trust between state and society to address the estrangement created since 2003.

brief.summary: The article, drawn from interviews with Sunni Arab figures in Iraq, argues that Sunnis feel politically marginalised despite holding formal government and parliamentary seats. Interviewees describe Shiite parties, many tied to armed factions, as controlling security and key decisions, with the 'anti-corruption' drive seen as targeting Sunni provinces. They say militias such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq and al-Nujaba have shifted from street power to economic control, and that Popular Mobilisation Forces units block displaced Sunnis from returning, notably to Jurf al-Sakhar. Sources split on the US-led coalition's withdrawal: some see it as a tactical move against militias, others expect Washington to lack the leverage to disarm them. Several voice fears of limited Islamic State cell attacks, though none expect a large-scale sectarian war.
brief.argument: Sunni Arabs in Iraq feel excluded from real decision-making, and armed factions tied to Iran are entrenching economic and political power that the state has not checked, which the authors see as a threat to stability.
recommendations: Bring all armed groups under effective state control and make disarmament deadlines enforceable
Allow displaced Sunni residents, especially in Jurf al-Sakhar, to return, addressing security concerns through law and individual accountability
Ensure Sunni representation translates into real influence in security and military appointments

title: Why Kazakhstan Joined Both the American and Chinese AI Initiatives
summary: Kazakhstan did not choose between Washington’s Pax Silica and Beijing’s WAICO: it joined both. It needs technology from both superpowers, and a say in the rules.

ai.sum: Kazakhstan joined both the US-led Pax Silica and China's WAICO AI initiatives to access technology from both and shape rules.

brief.summary: The author argues that Kazakhstan joined both the US-led Pax Silica initiative and China-led WAICO because it needs technology from both superpowers and a voice in the rules, rather than choosing sides. Pragmatism drives this: the US and China hold the leading AI capabilities, while Kazakhstan offers leverage through uranium and critical minerals such as tungsten. Its AI push, framed as both a state-efficiency tool and an export industry, relies on American chips and data centres, Chinese connectivity and models, Russian internet routes and nuclear power, and UAE partnerships, with European influence in its legal framework. The author also contends that neither initiative provides the testing and governance capacity needed, since that ability sits mainly inside frontier AI firms. Tokayev's proposals for common standards and an expert platform are described as capabilities that exist nowhere yet, making binding rules increasingly important for smaller states.
brief.argument: Kazakhstan joins both US and Chinese AI initiatives because it needs their technology and wants a say in the rules, and neither initiative yet supplies the governance capacity it requires.
recommendations: Establish common standards for testing and certifying AI systems
Create a permanent expert platform on AI regulation and ethics
Ensure WAICO and Pax Silica develop rules that constrain the strong, not only bilateral bargains

title: Sicherheit vor Demokratie & Nachtreten beim Bas-Rücktritt
Could Flávio Bolsonaro Deliver on His Fiscal Promises?
summary: Investors are betting that the Brazilian presidential candidate will rein in public debt. But structural and political hurdles make austerity easier to promise than to enact.

ai.sum: Analysis argues investors expect Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro to curb public debt, though structural and political obstacles make it hard.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Brazilian markets have priced in a belief that presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro will deliver fiscal austerity, as bond yields fell, the real strengthened and CDS spreads tightened whenever his lead grew. They contend this optimism is premature. Brazil's gross debt is near 83 percent of GDP and interest costs take 8.8 percent of GDP, yet most spending is mandatory, his promised roughly $40 billion adjustment lacks detail, and his growth pledges (tax cuts, infrastructure, state debt buyouts) pull the other way. Coalition bargaining and social spending pressures further complicate reform. Drawing on Lula, Erdogan, López Obrador and Bolsonaro's own record, they conclude populists usually adopt austerity only under crisis, so Brazilian assets should be viewed sceptically.
brief.argument: Markets are pricing in Flávio Bolsonaro's fiscal austerity pledges, but structural constraints and political pressures make those promises hard to deliver once in office.

title: President John F. Kennedy Tells the World That Soviet Missiles Are in Cuba (Cuban Missile Crisis, Day Seven)

ai.sum: Historical item: Kennedy announces a US naval quarantine of Cuba over Soviet missiles, Day Seven of the crisis.

brief.summary: James M. Lindsay recounts Day Seven of the Cuban Missile Crisis, 22 October 1962, when President Kennedy disclosed Soviet nuclear-tipped missiles in Cuba. He narrates the briefings given to US lawmakers, including the hawkish reactions of Senators Russell and Fulbright, and a call with Eisenhower who backed the response. He then covers allied briefings, with de Gaulle accepting Kennedy's word and Diefenbaker proving hostile, and a brief scare when Gromyko's announcement proved routine. The article closes with Kennedy's speech, the announced quarantine, the raised DEFCON levels and the mobilisation of bombers. The piece is a republished historical essay on the 250th anniversary series, not a policy paper.
brief.argument: Kennedy's public disclosure and quarantine were a deliberate move to seize the initiative before Moscow could pre-empt him, and the manner of briefing allies and Congress shaped the crisis's political management.

title: Whoever wins the election , Israel illiberal turn is here to stay – European Council on Foreign Relations

ai.sum: ECFR analysis argues Israel's illiberal political turn will persist regardless of the outcome of the upcoming election.

brief.summary: The authors argue that whatever the outcome of Israel's October 2026 election, the country's illiberal, hard-right shift will persist, because it has been embedded in key institutions beyond Netanyahu himself. They map five possible post-election scenarios, from deadlock and caretaker rule to minority or unity governments, and conclude that an opposition-led government would ease domestic measures such as the judicial overhaul and the October 7 inquiry, but would keep Israel's post-October 7 security doctrine, settlement expansion and rejection of Palestinian statehood largely intact. They expect little change in foreign policy, with some easing in Gaza and the West Bank and a possible Syria security pact but no diplomatic track with the Palestinians. They advise Europeans to set out conditions privately, make the costs of continued expansion clear publicly, and be ready to use political and economic leverage if Israel does not change course.
brief.argument: Israel's illiberal, ethno-nationalist drift will continue regardless of who wins the election, because it is rooted in institutions and policy consensus beyond Netanyahu.
recommendations: Set out conditions for resetting bilateral ties privately once the new government is formed
Make publicly clear the costs and benefits of diplomacy versus territorial expansion and military aggression
Prepare to use political and economic leverage, such as measures against the settlement project, if Israel does not change tack

title: Israel’s Election: Who’s Who and What’s at Stake?
summary: Israel’s October 27 election could reshape the country’s political landscape, but neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies nor the opposition has a clear path to a governing majority. The outcome of the vote could determine not only who leads Israel, but how the country contends with various domestic and foreign policy concerns.

ai.sum: Israel's October 27 election may not produce a clear governing majority for Netanyahu's allies or the opposition.

brief.summary: The CFR piece, drawing on experts Elliott Abrams and Steven A. Cook, frames Israel's October 27 election as possibly among the most consequential in the country's history. The authors explain Israel's proportional system, the 3.25 percent threshold and the 61-seat majority requirement, and map the two blocs: the Netanyahu coalition and an anti-Netanyahu 'change bloc' that has not agreed on a successor. They argue neither side has a clear path to 61 seats, so a government may depend on concessions such as a rotational premiership, sitting with Arab parties, or sitting with ultra-Orthodox parties, and that prolonged negotiations or a further election are plausible. On foreign policy, the authors expect little abrupt change; a new government would mainly alter tone, possibly toward settler violence in the West Bank and relations with Jordan.
brief.argument: Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition has a clear route to a 61-seat majority, so coalition arithmetic will force hard concessions and may produce a further election, while foreign policy would change mainly in tone rather than substance.

title: The US-Israel relationship needs a reset. Here’s how to do it.
summary: A new Israeli government could offer a chance to reset strained relations with Washington. The post The US-Israel relationship needs a reset. Here’s how to do it. appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis argues a new Israeli government could offer a chance to reset strained US-Israel relations.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the US-Israel alliance is at once at a high point operationally and eroding politically, and that it needs a deliberate reset. They point to joint operations against Iran and the hostage deal as proof of strength, but cite Israeli government decisions (freezing Gaza 'day after' planning, West Bank violence, partisan alignment), US Congressional votes and falling public support as sources of strain. Their remedy is a seven-pillar roadmap: shared democratic values and bipartisanship, a diplomatic initiative on Gaza, the Palestinians, Lebanon, Syria and Saudi normalisation, a transition from aid to partnership in the next MOU from 2029, Israel as a regional air-defence hub, a deeper defence-industrial partnership, cooperation on AI and space, and a institutionalised Strategic Dialogue run by professionals. The piece is written by a former head of Israel's Defense Ministry Political-Military Bureau.
brief.argument: The US-Israel alliance is operationally stronger than ever but politically fraying, so it needs a structured reset that shifts it from aid to partnership while restoring institutional anchors.
recommendations: Implement the current 2019-2028 MOU in full and phase the shift from aid to partnership in the next MOU from 2029, offset by joint R&D and co-production
Lead a structured Israeli diplomatic initiative on Gaza demilitarisation, a Palestinian political horizon designed with Washington, and an end to West Bank extremist violence
Modernise export-control arrangements and advance the defence-industrial working group and FUTURES Act cooperation
Create a multi-year Strategic Dialogue co-chaired by the US national security advisor and the head of Israel's National Security Council, staffed by career professionals
brief.turkey: The proposed Israeli-US realignment on Gaza, Syria, Lebanon and Saudi normalisation, plus a regional air-defence hub, would reshape the regional order in which Türkiye operates and could shift its relative position with Washington.

brief.summary: The piece tells the story of two Marine veterans, Jeff Lindquist and Erik Won, who served together in Iraq. After Lindquist lost fellow Marines there, he struggled with post-traumatic stress that was steadily wrecking his life. The authors describe how an innovative treatment, Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), using synchronized transcranial magnetic stimulation, helped him recover. Their account frames his recovery as the first step in a wider effort, led with Won, to bring the same treatment to other veterans with post-traumatic stress. The text is a personal narrative and advocacy piece rather than an analytical study, and the excerpt provided is cut off before the full argument on the therapy's effectiveness is developed.
brief.argument: A veteran's recovery from post-traumatic stress through an advanced brain-stimulation therapy can become the basis for a broader effort to help other veterans.

ai.sum: Washington issued a new arrest warrant for Raúl Castro amid Cuba's worsening economic and humanitarian crisis.

brief.summary: The authors argue that a new arrest warrant for Raúl Castro, tied to the 1996 shoot-down of two Brothers to the Rescue aircraft, signals US seriousness about accountability, even though it will not soon bring him into custody. They describe Cuba's economic and humanitarian collapse as worsened by lost trade, the drying up of Venezuelan oil after Maduro's removal, and US sanctions. They contend that the regime prioritises keeping power over the welfare of Cubans, that its economic reforms are a charade, and that only a complete political transition, including dismantling the security structure and establishing democracy, can serve both US security goals and Cuban welfare. They say early planning for post-transition reconstruction with international financial institutions and the exile community should begin now, and that Cuban opposition groups grouped under the Freedom Accord should have a seat in any serious negotiation.
brief.argument: Lasting change in Cuba requires a complete political transition that dismantles the regime's security structure, with Washington's pressure and accountability measures supporting it.
recommendations: Continue direct messaging to the Cuban people about a post-regime economic model
Systematically sanction current Cuban leaders and pursue legal accountability
Begin early planning and initial funding commitments with international financial institutions and partners for post-transition reconstruction
Give Cuban pro-democracy groups, including the Freedom Accord coalition, a place in any serious negotiation
